name: The Broken Windows Theory
statement: Visible disorder invites more disorder, and eventually serious crime.
meaning: Broken windows theory holds that visible signs of disorder and minor offences — broken windows, graffiti, litter, vandalism — signal that a place is unwatched and uncared-for, which invites further disorder and, ultimately, more serious crime. Its corollary is that promptly fixing small problems and maintaining public order interrupts the slide. The metaphor: one unrepaired broken window signals that no one cares, so breaking the rest costs nothing.
mechanism: The theorized chain runs through social signalling and informal control. Visible disorder communicates that no one is minding the place and that norms go unenforced, which emboldens would-be offenders and breeds fear among residents. Frightened residents withdraw from public space, which weakens the informal social control that once kept order, opening a feedback loop in which disorder and eventually serious crime accumulate. Fixing the small signs, on this view, breaks the loop before it starts.

examples.text: A car left without plates was stripped within a day in the Bronx but sat untouched for a week in Palo Alto — until Zimbardo smashed it himself, after which passersby joined in, the precursor experiment the theory drew on.
Order-maintenance policing under Bratton and Giuliani in 1990s New York, targeting fare evasion and graffiti, was credited by proponents with the city's crime decline.

Keizer and colleagues found that visible graffiti and litter measurably increased other norm-breaking, including littering and even petty theft — support for the narrow disorder-spreads-disorder mechanism.

variants.name: Order-maintenance versus zero tolerance
variants.text: The gentler order-maintenance policing Kelling emphasised, stressing officer discretion, versus the harder zero-tolerance version applied in practice — often conflated but not the same.

variants.name: Collective efficacy
variants.text: Sampson and Raudenbush's rival account, in which disorder and crime are both products of weak neighbourhood cohesion and shared willingness to intervene, making the disorder-crime link largely spurious.

whyItMatters: It became one of the most influential ideas in criminology and urban policy, the intellectual basis for order-maintenance and zero-tolerance policing in cities around the world. Its contested evidence and its association with over-policing have made it equally influential as a cautionary case in debates over what actually reduces crime and at what cost.

working.text: distinguish whether disorder spreads disorder, which has some support, from whether such policing reduces serious crime, which is disputed.
resist crediting any single policy with a crime decline that coincided with many other changes, as in 1990s New York.
set any claimed benefit against the documented harms of over-policing, racial disparities, and the criminalisation of poverty.

limits: The theory is heavily contested, and two claims must be kept apart. That minor disorder spreads more minor disorder has genuine experimental support. But that broken-windows policing reduces serious crime, and that it caused New York's decline, is disputed and confounded: crime fell across most American cities in the 1990s, including those that never adopted it, amid the end of the crack epidemic, economic growth, more police, and other shifts. A major randomised study found families moved to lower-disorder neighbourhoods did not commit fewer crimes. And the approach is tied to over-policing, racial disparities, and stop-and-frisk abuses found unconstitutional.
misreadings: Broken windows is not the same as zero tolerance — Kelling stressed discretion, while the harder version was often applied in practice. The New York crime drop does not prove the theory, since crime fell nationally, including where the policy was never used. The Dutch experiments support only that minor disorder breeds more minor disorder, not the escalation to serious crime or the policing prescription. And the disorder-crime link may be largely explained by an underlying common cause, weak collective efficacy.
origin: Introduced by James Q. Wilson and George Kelling in 'Broken Windows' (The Atlantic Monthly, 1982), drawing on Philip Zimbardo's abandoned-car experiments; applied to policing in 1990s New York and contested by later studies, including Harcourt and Ludwig's analysis of a five-city housing experiment.
namedAfter: James Q. Wilson and George Kelling

sources.text: Wilson & Kelling, "Broken Windows," The Atlantic Monthly (1982). — the founding article and the metaphor.
Keizer, Lindenberg & Steg, "The Spreading of Disorder," Science 322(5908):1681-1685 (2008). — field experiments supporting the disorder-spreads-disorder mechanism.

Harcourt & Ludwig, "Broken Windows: New Evidence from New York City and a Five-City Social Experiment," University of Chicago Law Review 73(1):271-320 (2006). — little causal support for the crime-reduction claim.
